newsitem.title: USA: Judge holds off decision on Florida tobacco case.
newsitem.headline: Judge holds off decision on Florida tobacco case.

text.p: A Florida judge heard arguments but did not rule Tuesday on a bid by Brown & Williamson Tobacco Corp. to overturn a jury award of $750,000 to a smoker with lung cancer.

A lawyer for Brown & Williamson, a unit of B.A.T Industries PLC, argued that an Aug. 9 judgment in favour of Grady Carter of Orange Park, Fla., was erroneous, claiming internal company documents were improperly admitted as evidence.

In the August ruling, a six-member circuit court jury decided that Brown & Williamson was negligent and made a dangerous and defective product. The judgment was just the second rendered against the tobacco industry and sent shock waves through the market, causing tobacco stocks to plunge.

Carter, a 66-yer-old retired air traffic controller, smoked Lucky Strikes cigarettes, made by American Tobacco Co., from 1947 until 1972, when he switched to other brands. American was merged into Brown & Williamson in 1995.

Brown & Williamson, in its petition Tuesday, asked for a directed verdict, issued by the judge in a jury trial without consideration by the jury, or a new trial. Duval County Circuit Judge Brian Davis did not say when he would rule.

Brown & Williamson attorney Thomas Riley told Davis Tuesday that Carter's allegations were based on his smoking during a time when American and Brown & Williamson were rivals, but that the judge had effectively allowed Carter's lawyers to put the conduct of Brown & Williamson on trial by permitting internal company documents to be entered as evidence.
"The jury was invited to assess liability based on what Brown & Williamson did or did not do," said Riley.
Among the documents presented at trial was a 1963 memo in which former Brown & Williamson general counsel Addison Yeaman indicated nicotine was an addictive drug.
Riley claimed the document should have been protected by attorney-client privilege. "They made Yeaman a witness against his own client," he said.

But Norwood Wilner, attorney for Carter, argued that Brown & Williamson opened the door to presentation of the documents by taking a current position -- that cigarettes are not addictive -- that differed from the position espoused in their internal documents of three decades ago.
Even if Yeaman was acting as an attorney for the company at the time, Wilner said, "the nature of what they were doing was to defraud the public."

Riley also argued that Carter should not have been allowed to testify as to what he might have done had the company issued a warning about the possible effects of smoking. Lawyers for Carter argued at trial that tobacco companies deliberately hid the dangers of smoking.
"There's no proof that a warning would have deterred Mr. Carter from smoking," he said.
Riley also said the company was denied proper notice of the evidence to be presented at trial and did not have time to assemble a case.
"There are a lot of things that we could have done that we were never given the opportunity to do," he said.
Riley said if the ruling went against Brown & Williamson, the company would appeal to the state's First District Court of Appeals.
The Carter case was just the second product liability case in which a judgment had been rendered against the tobacco industry. In 1988 a jury awarded $400,000 to the family of Rose Cipollone.
Although a federal appeals court overturned the Cipollone verdict, the U.S. Supreme Court found the lower court erred.
The nation's highest court then issued the 1992 landmark ruling that the federally mandated warning on cigarette packages did not protect tobacco companies from personal injury suits.

The Supreme Court sent the Cipollone case back for retrial in New Jersey, but the suit was dropped when the law firm that had been representing the plaintiffs could no longer afford to fight the tobacco industry.
On the American Stock Exchange, BAT American depositary shares fell 6.25 cents to $14.
